phase1.explanation:
Every window you've built so far has been hand-nailed together in Java: new Label(), new VBox(), getChildren().add(). [[term:FXML]] is the alternative — the interior designer's blueprint, written as its own separate file, instead of construction instructions buried inside your program logic.

FXML is exactly what the name says: [[term:F]]X [[term:M]]ark[[term:L]]anguage — an XML dialect where each tag is a JavaFX class (<VBox>, <Button>, <Label>) and each attribute is a property (text="Click Me"). A [[term:FXMLLoader]] reads that file at runtime and builds the exact same scene graph you'd otherwise build by hand in Java — same Stage, same Scene, same nodes, just described declaratively instead of imperatively constructed.

The payoff is separation: your layout lives in one file, your logic lives in a separate [[term:controller]] class, connected by the [[term:@FXML]] annotation (which we'll wire up properly next lesson). [[key:that split means a designer can rearrange the window without touching a line of Java, and a developer can rewrite the button's behavior without touching the layout]] — the same kind of clean separation encapsulation gave you back in Unit 1, just applied to UI instead of data.

[[term:Scene Builder]] is Oracle's drag-and-drop tool for editing FXML visually instead of hand-typing tags — [[fun:it generates the exact same FXML file a human would write by hand]], it's purely a convenience layer, not a separate technology.

phase2.explanation:
No broken code — conceptual lesson. Two misconceptions worth clearing up before we wire up a real controller next lesson.

"FXML replaces Java code" — [[warn:not quite]]. FXML replaces the *construction* code — the new Label(), getChildren().add() calls — but you still write a Java controller class for behavior (what happens on a click, how data gets validated). FXML and Java split the job; neither replaces the other.

"You need Scene Builder to use FXML" — also not true. [[key:FXML is just a text file]]; you can write it by hand in any editor, the same way you could hand-write HTML without a visual page builder. Scene Builder just makes the process faster and more visual — it's optional tooling, not a requirement of the format.

mcq.question:
Which statement about FXML is TRUE?

A) FXML files are written in HTML
B) The @FXML annotation is used to bind UI elements to controller fields
C) FXML can only be created with Scene Builder
D) FXML makes JavaFX applications slower

Select the CORRECT statement.

phase5.trivia: [[fun:FXMLLoader builds the scene graph using reflection]] — it reads a tag like <Button text="OK"/>, looks up the javafx.scene.control.Button class by name, calls its no-arg constructor, and then calls the matching setText("OK") setter it finds by convention. That's the same reflective pattern PropertyValueFactory uses in TableView, coming up a couple lessons from now.
